A DATA STORY · WHO LIFE EXPECTANCY, 183 COUNTRIES, 2000–2015
Can you predict how long people live?
A machine-learning model that estimates a country’s life expectancy from 13 health and economic statistics, tested honestly on countries it had never seen, and taken apart to find out where it fails and why.
Scott Schirkofsky · schirko.com/scott/life-expectancy
THE QUESTION
From a handful of statistics, can you tell how long people in a country will live?
The data
World Health Organization figures for 183 countries, every year from 2000 to 2015. One row is one country in one year: 2,928 rows.
The inputs
13 statistics: deaths (adult mortality, HIV/AIDS, under-fives), immunization rates, nutrition, health spending, schooling and an income-development index.
The answer we want
Average life expectancy at birth, in years. It runs from 36 to 89 in this data.
And the harder question: how do you know the answer is any good?
Can you predict how long people live?
2
THE DATA
The data looked clean. It wasn’t.
22%
Blank, the obvious kind
Population is blank in 22% of rows, hepatitis B in 19%, GDP in 15%. Easy to see, easy to handle.
606
Zeros that mean “not reported”
Health spending is exactly 0 in 606 rows. Nobody spends nothing on health. A blank-value check calls these complete.
49%
Impossible values
Half of all average-BMI figures are outside 10–50, which no population can have. The column was dropped.
Plus six advanced economies, Canada and France among them, tagged “Developing”.
Notebook 1 · The data
3
THE DATA
In 2015, 181 of 183 countries “spent nothing” on health
The same 26 countries report zero every year, and then almost everyone does in 2015. That is a reporting gap, not a fact.
The fix: a zero in this column now counts as missing, and gets filled from the country’s own earlier years.
It changed the model’s accuracy by less than a hundredth of a year. It was still worth doing: a model should not learn from values known to be wrong.
Notebook 2 · Cleaning
4
THE HONEST TEST
The same country appears 16 times. A random test lets the model peek.
The usual test: hold back random rows
Train on 80% of rows, predict the rest. But Brazil 2012 is in the test set while Brazil 2011 and 2013 are in training, and they are nearly identical. The model is filling in a missing year for a country it knows.
The honest test: hold back whole countries
Split by country, not by row. Train on 146 countries, predict all 16 years of the other 37, five times over. Every country is predicted once while completely unseen.
How you test is part of the answer.
Notebook 3 · The honest test
5
THE HONEST TEST
Two scores for one model. The second one is true.
R² is the share of the variation the model explains; 1.0 is perfect. Average miss is how many years off a typical prediction is.
On a country it has never seen, the model is within about 2 years and explains 90% of the variation. Strong, but the random test overstated accuracy by nearly a factor of two in years.
The project reports both, and explains the gap.
Notebook 3 · The honest test
6
WHAT THE MODEL LEARNED
Three inputs do almost all the work
Scramble one input into noise and see how much worse the model gets. HIV/AIDS deaths, adult mortality and the income-development index each cost it 0.2 or more of its R². The other ten cost 0.02 or less.
That matches what is known: HIV drove the lowest life expectancies of the period, and the income index captures the development gap. The model found real signals, not a shortcut.
Notebook 4 · What drives the predictions
7
WHAT THE MODEL LEARNED
Any serious HIV burden costs about seven years, five of them at once
Slide one input from low to high, hold everything else fixed, and watch the prediction. For HIV/AIDS deaths there is a cliff at about 0.5 per 1,000: the prediction drops five years almost at once, then slides a little further.
This is not a straight line, which is why a simple linear model scores clearly worse (slide 13).
Notebook 4 · What drives the predictions
8
WHERE IT FAILS
The error is not spread evenly. A few countries carry it.
The typical country is missed by 2.0 years. The worst 10% of countries carry 22% of all the error.
Predicted too high: Somalia, Sierra Leone, Angola, Côte d’Ivoire, Swaziland. The shortest lives in the data, several marked by conflict or epidemics.
Predicted too low: Korea, Cuba, Guatemala. They live longer than their statistics suggest.
Somalia has no data at all for four inputs. For the rest, missing data is not the explanation.
Notebook 5 · Where the model fails
9
WHERE IT FAILS
The pattern looks fixable. It isn’t, and here is why.
Left: sliced by the true value, the shortest-lived countries are predicted 2.5 years too high. Tempting: “lower the low predictions a bit.”
Right: sliced by the prediction, which is all you have for a new country, the bias vanishes. Among countries predicted at 60, some are really 50 and some 70, and the model cannot tell which.
Fitted corrections, tested fairly, made the average miss worse (2.14 → 2.21 years).
Notebook 5 · Where the model fails
10
IS IT FAIR?
Developing countries are missed by more, even like for like
0.41
years: the gap
Developed countries are missed by 1.8 years on average, developing by 2.2. Six mislabelled countries were moved first; that alone shrank the gap from 0.54.
99%
of redraws keep it
Redraw the set of countries 2,000 times: the gap stays above zero in over 99% of them. It is not a fluke of which countries happened to be in the data.
0.6
years, like for like
Among countries living 75–80 years, developing ones are still missed by 0.6 years more. The gap is not just “a harder group”.
Modest, consistent, and not fixable from these inputs. The likely cause is reporting quality. It is recorded as a limitation, not hidden.
Notebook 6 · Fairness
11
IS IT FAIR?
The uncertainty band promised 80%. For developing countries it delivered 76%.
Each prediction comes with a range, from the spread of the 200 trees, meant to hold the truth 80% of the time. It did for developed countries; for developing countries it was overconfident.
The fix is to stretch the band 13% wider for developing countries, learned on some countries and tested on others. Now 81% and 80%. The price is honesty, not accuracy.
Notebook 6 · The uncertainty band
12
WHAT DIDN’T HELP
A better algorithm didn’t help. Neither did tuning.
Four algorithms, same honest test: the three tree models tie at R² 0.90. Linear regression is clearly worse because the relationships bend, like the HIV cliff.
All four fail on the same countries. Six are in the worst 18 for every model; Somalia is missed by 9–12 years by all of them.
Tuning 36 combinations of the forest’s settings: +0.001 R².
Notebook 7 · What didn’t help
13
THE VERDICT
The method is not the bottleneck. The inputs are.
90%
of what decides a country’s life expectancy is in 13 WHO statistics.
Different algorithms: tied. Different settings: +0.001. Corrections afterwards: worse. Three independent lines of evidence point the same way.
The remaining 10% lives in things the table does not measure: conflict, epidemics, and how reliable each country’s reporting is.
That is where the hardest countries are, and that is where the next improvement has to come from.
Notebooks 5–7
14
WHAT WOULD HELP
Better information, not a better algorithm
1. Outside data on conflict and epidemics
Armed-conflict and epidemic indicators for the period, joined by country and year, and tested the same honest way: whole countries held out.
2. A reporting-quality signal
How much of each country’s data was filled in, and how stable its figures are year to year, as inputs. The fairness gap suggests this is where the noise lives.
3. Keep the honest test
Any gain has to show on unseen countries. On the random-row test, almost anything looks like an improvement.
If asked “how would you improve this?” the answer is not a fancier model. It is better data for the countries where the model struggles.

HOW IT WAS BUILT
Everything on the project page can be reproduced from the repository
The pipeline
Python, pandas and scikit-learn. A random forest of 200 trees with outlier clipping built into the model, so no test row ever shapes it. Settings live in one YAML file, so a similar dataset swaps in without code changes.
Checked, not just claimed
36 automated tests run on every push: the cleaning rules, the leak-free clipping, the honest split, and that the page and docs quote the same numbers as the saved results.
Documented for a non-analyst
Seven notebooks walk through the project in order, each step as “what we are looking for, the code and its result, how to read it, what it means, what’s next and why”. A findings page, a plain-English glossary and a build log of every milestone and why.
